# zero-server engineering rules

These rules bind every change in this repository, whoever or whatever makes
it. They are the project's working agreement, kept here so a session that
starts from a fresh clone has them.

## Stack and layout

- Cargo workspace at the repository root; capability crates under `crates/`
  (one responsibility per crate, named `zero-<capability>`); the bundle crate
  is `crates/zero-server`; the C ABI is `crates/zero-ffi` (cbindgen header
  `include/zero.h`, regenerated on every build).
- `bindings/node` (napi-rs, `@zero-server/*`), `bindings/python` (PyO3 plus
  hatchling, `zero-server-*`), `bindings/dotnet` (`[LibraryImport]`,
  `ZeroServer.*`): standalone crates and projects excluded from the workspace,
  built by their own pipelines.
- `conformance/vectors.json` is generated by
  `cargo run -p zero-examples --example conformance_vectors` and asserted by all
  three bindings; `conformance/api-surface.json` is the export contract.
- `docs/standards.toml` is the conformance registry; `docs/capabilities.toml`
  claims every library crate exactly once; `docs/lints/*.toml` are the three
  lint tables `cargo xtask lints --check` enforces.
- `crates/xtask` is the task runner (`cargo xtask <task>`); `crates/zero-bench`
  holds the TechEmpower entries and the measurement gates and is never
  published.

## Commands

- Build: `cargo build --workspace`; test: `cargo test --workspace`; no_std:
  `just nostd` (or the `cargo check -p <crate> --no-default-features` loop over
  the no_std crates listed in `docs/capabilities.toml`).
- Lint: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; format check:
  `cargo fmt --all -- --check`.
- Everything CI runs: `just ci`; task list: `cargo xtask`.
- Bench: `just bench <entry>` (Linux host or container).

Do not hand-guess rustfmt output: it rewraps at fn_call_width (about 60
columns), not only at max_width. A crate is immutable once on crates.io, so
the fmt and clippy job must be green before any publish.

## Standards-first

- Every feature maps to a row in `docs/standards.toml` (RFCs at
  rfc-editor.org, W3C and WHATWG specs, protobuf.dev, the gRPC PROTOCOL-HTTP2
  document, Prometheus exposition format, W3C Trace Context, NIST SP 800-63B,
  OWASP cheat sheets, the vendor reference for each database dialect).
- Before implementing, changing or reviewing any protocol, wire format,
  parser, header, cookie, crypto or auth behavior: fetch the cited source
  live, read the section, and work from that text. Never implement standards
  behavior from memory. No row: add one first and fetch it.
- Cite the source in code (`@see <url>#section` in the rustdoc of the item
  that implements it) and in the commit body. Conformance tests are named
  after the statement they check and carry the section number; every row
  carries a `release` field and `cargo xtask standards --check` enforces the
  rows at or below the current release.
- Only the current document counts (RFC 9110 to 9112 not 2616 or 7230 to
  7235; RFC 9113 not 7540; RFC 8489 not 5389; RFC 8656 not 5766). Update the
  row when a source is obsoleted.
- Security defaults follow the standard's MUST and SHOULD plus the referenced
  BCP (RFC 8725 for JWT, RFC 9700 for OAuth 2.0, rfc6265bis for cookies).
  Deviations require a rationale in the rustdoc and a test that pins the
  behavior.

## Dependencies and unsafe

- Zero third-party crates in every crate that neither terminates TLS, hosts
  QUIC, sits on the runtime seam, makes raw OS calls, wraps the C library nor
  crosses a language boundary. The others carry the pinned allowlist in
  `deny.toml` (and `deny/*.toml` for the bindings and feature graphs); any
  crate not listed is denied.
- `unsafe_code = "forbid"` everywhere except the audited crates (zero-simd,
  zero-server-crypto, zero-ffi, zero-sys, zero-sqlite, zero-plugin,
  bindings/node, bindings/python/packages/native), which use `deny` with
  per-item allows and a `// SAFETY:` comment on every block.
- no_std crates carry `#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]`,
  `extern crate alloc`, the no_std lint table (no indexing, unwrap, expect,
  panic or unchecked arithmetic), and build with `--no-default-features` on
  the host and for thumbv7em-none-eabihf in CI.
- Installing any binding never compiles anything: prebuilt binaries for the
  seven targets in the release workflows; native code is never a build-time
  requirement of a user.

## Currency (no stale versions or facts)

- Training knowledge is expired for anything with a date: versions,
  end-of-life dates, API signatures, feature names, action tags, image tags,
  prices. Fetch such a fact live before writing it, and put the URL and the
  date of the fetch in the commit body.
- Versions come from the registry, never from memory: crates.io
  `https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/<name>` (`max_stable_version`, `yanked`,
  `updated_at`), npm `https://registry.npmjs.org/<name>/latest`, PyPI
  `https://pypi.org/pypi/<name>/json`, NuGet
  `https://api.nuget.org/v3-flatcontainer/<id>/index.json`, GitHub Actions
  and Docker images from their releases or tags page. Pin what the registry
  returned today; a version written without a fetch is a defect, and so is
  `latest` in any manifest or workflow.
- Read the documentation of the pinned version, not the newest:
  `https://docs.rs/<crate>/<version>`, the package README at the pinned tag,
  the Node API docs for the pinned `engines` line, the Rust release notes for
  the pinned `rust-version`. An API the pinned docs do not show does not
  exist; do not call it.
- Before a crate enters `deny.toml`: not yanked, no open RUSTSEC advisory
  (`cargo deny check advisories`), repository not archived, a release within
  the last 12 months unless the crate is finished and says so, a stable line
  (no `0.x`, `beta` or `rc`) unless the design records why. Write the check
  date in the comment beside the allow entry; an entry older than 180 days is
  rechecked before the next release.
- Support windows are fetched, not assumed: Node from
  nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases, Python from
  devguide.python.org/versions, .NET from
  dotnet.microsoft.com/platform/support/policy, Rust from the release notes,
  GitHub runners from the actions/runner-images changelog. Every `engines`,
  `requires-python`, `TargetFramework`, `rust-version` and `runs-on` value
  cites the page and date it was checked against.
- A fetch that fails is reported as unverified, in the reply and in the
  commit body, never replaced by a remembered value. Stale means any of: the
  document is obsoleted, the pinned version is behind the registry's stable
  line by a major, or a moving fact was last checked more than 90 days ago.
- `cargo update`, `npm update`, `pip` and NuGet bumps and dependabot merges
  are deliberate commits that link the changelog of every bumped package; a
  lockfile never changes as a side effect of other work.

## Testing

- No fixed sleeps to wait for an assertion: poll, use fake time, or await the
  real event. Every bug fix ships with a test that fails on the previous
  code.
- Parsers of untrusted input carry proptest tests and a libFuzzer target and
  never panic on arbitrary bytes. Tests anchor to the specification's own
  vectors, not to round-trips alone.
- `Cargo.lock` is committed in the workspace and in every binding; `npm ci`
  and `cargo vet` must pass from the committed lockfiles. Linux-only failures
  are reproduced in a container before code changes.

## Conventions

- American English everywhere (color, behavior, license, catalog, serialize,
  analyze, artifact, canceled, judgment, while). Regular dashes only; no em or
  en dashes; no horizontal rules.
- Rust follows rustfmt's default style; TypeScript and C# use Allman braces.
- Rustdoc with `# Arguments`, `# Returns`, `# Errors` on every public item;
  `missing_docs` is denied; crate READMEs, `include/zero.h`, `index.d.ts`,
  `__init__.pyi` and `conformance/vectors.json` are generated: edit the source
  and regenerate, never the artifact.
- Comments sparse; module headers and public-item docs only; no inline
  narration.
- No planning vocabulary in code, docs or commits (no iteration labels, no
  numbered plan references). Describe the change and its reason in
  professional engineering terms. The one place planning vocabulary is
  allowed is this folder, `.github/cloud/`, which is the plan.
- Examples and guides build values with library calls; never paste byte
  blobs.
- Every change that ships or removes a capability audits `web/home.toml`, the
  README and the capability and standards pages in the same commit.
- Public text (the README, the site, package pages, crate docs, the profile
  card) makes no performance claim except a measured one, and names another
  project only as an entry measured beside zero-server (owner decision,
  2026-10-01). A published figure comes from a committed run: the median of
  five interleaved runs on the stated hardware, the ratio against each entry
  measured in the same session beside the absolute number, every error counter
  at zero, the raw data and the command that reproduces it in the repository,
  and every entry built and configured the way its own project documents for
  production (its own TechEmpower entry where one exists). Targets,
  projections and figures taken from other sources stay in the plan
  (`.github/cloud/`). Public text describes only what exists, and states
  plainly what does not exist yet.
- Commits: short imperative subject, optional body that states the change and
  its reason, authored as molexxxx, no assistant or AI attribution of any
  kind, no co-author trailers, nothing that names the tooling that produced
  the change. Push to `origin main`; never force-push; never rewrite history.
- Secrets never enter the tree. `.env` files, tokens and keys are never read
  into a commit, a log or a document.
